title: The existential cure for the mental health crisis
subtitle: Why existential therapy works
author: Emmy van Deurzen
introduction: As the world lurches from one crisis to the next, an invisible epidemic spreads — disillusionment, despair, and a quiet surrender to meaninglessness. Modern psychiatry often seeks to medicate away this dread, but what if the real cure lies not in avoidance but in confrontation? Existential therapy uses philosophical thinking to ask the hard questions — about life, death, purpose, and courage — guiding us through the abyss to find a path worth taking.
body:
The dying of the light

In a world that is confronting one major crisis after another, it has become critical to address the despair and despondency that are more and more widespread. Many people are confronted with serious doubts about the meaning of their lives. Many young people have become skeptical and cynical about human existence in general. This kind of nihilism can easily lead to an experience of existential crisis, during which you feel uncontainable anxiety, depression or despair, as it seems as if your world and safety are crumbling or imploding. Such symptoms are usually rapidly medicalized, and the person’s concerns are frequently treated as a mental health problem, which is attributed to malfunctioning of the brain. But medical or psychological approaches often fail to get to the core of the discontent and desolation. Is it any wonder that so many people feel confused, lose their bearings or give up all together on seeking meaning, preferring mindless distractions and hedonism? Is it strange that suicide figures around the world are alarmingly high?

Religious beliefs are also much less able to provide solace in what is now a predominantly secular society.

Sometimes, if the individual does not collapse into crisis, feelings of estrangement or disenfranchisement are channeled into anger and rebellion, which can turn into protest and aggression and fuel social unrest. This is not something that only affects those who are living through wars, droughts, floods and fires. It affects many people who are not directly involved in the dramas and trauma, but who are shaken by the changes in the world and who feel at a loss to make sense of any of it. Through the constant media presence in our lives, we are all exposed to what is happening around us in the world. None of us are exempt from observing and experiencing first-hand how civilization is faltering and failing. Many people feel deep compassion with victims of injustice, but do not see how they can remedy the situation.  Religious beliefs are also much less able to provide solace in what is now a predominantly secular society. Political solutions are harder to believe in, with autocracy and plutocracy so clearly on the rise.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Better left unsaid With Peter York, Theodore Dalrymple, Simon Wessely, Vanessa King

What are we to do?

Instead of giving up on human beings altogether or blaming everything on climate change or the new tide of fascism around the globe, or on the high numbers of immigration, it matters greatly that we stop and pause for mature reflection. If we are to build the emotional and moral resilience that is now required to face the situation we are in, we need to start by being clear about what is happening, not just in terms of the planet itself, but in terms of the mentality, beliefs and ideas of humanity. We can only truly rekindle hope for humankind on this planet by addressing the actual position squarely. Escaping to Mars is not a realistic option. How can we future proof our lives with the necessary strength, buoyancy and flexibility in dealing with the inexorable difficulties and challenges to come?

Where can we turn?

Existential philosophy is the kind of philosophy that asks big questions about human existence.  It is the philosophy that tackles the thorniest issues, such as the meaning of life, mortality, freedom, loneliness, truth, fairness, values and purpose. Existential philosophers are the thinkers who are therefore most experienced and expert at critically addressing these radical issues. From Moses to Zoroaster, to Heraclitus, Socrates, Plato, Confucius, Laozi, Aristotle, to Buddha, Jesus of Nazareth, Marcus Aurelius, Mohamed and Spinoza to Schopenhauer philosophers have sought to pinpoint reasons for living. More recent existential ideas proposed by people like Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Karl Jaspers, Fyodor Dostoyevsky, Leo Tolstoy, Martin Heidegger, Jean Paul Sartre, Frantz Fanon, Albert Camus, Simone de Beauvoir and Hannah Arendt, are even more adapted to penetrating to core problems in addressing the meaning of human existence.  Yet, all too often this thinking has remained academic, abstract, or dogmatic in nature, devoid of concrete relevance to ordinary people. Therefore, it is more sensible to turn to applied philosophy, in the form of existential psychotherapy, which has been developed over the past hundred years, in various parts of the world, by combining existential philosophy and psychology and by observing how we can best help people who are suffering and struggling in their everyday lives.

Why existential therapy?

One way in which existential therapy stands out from other forms of therapy is by breaking the taboo on mortality, directly addressing finitude and death.  The early Athenian philosophers, especially Socrates and Plato, spoke clearly about death and how important it was to face our fears of death, losses, failures and disappointments. They set great store by courage and confidence and the Stoics, especially the Roman branch, exemplified by Marcus Aurelius, provided guidance on some of the ways in which a person could build strength to live with more self-reliance and less dread.

When Ernest Becker wrote his book ‘The Denial of Death’ he showed that addressing the deep-seated human tendency to fear and avoid death and difficulty were one of the most pivotal challenges if we were to safeguard the future of humankind.

From Kierkegaard and Nietzsche onwards, existential philosophers returned to this challenge, and Heidegger’s and Sartre’s work were groundbreaking in speaking so centrally about death and nothingness. When Ernest Becker wrote his book ‘The Denial of Death’ he showed that addressing the deep-seated human tendency to fear and avoid death and difficulty were one of the most pivotal challenges if we were to safeguard the future of humankind. Viktor Frankl’s work grew directly out of his personal confrontation with death in the Holocaust.  Irv Yalom’s book ‘Existential Psychotherapy’ argued that death anxiety was at the root of most emotional problems, a bold claim that has been substantiated again and again.

Faced with new threats and darkness in the world it has become vital for existential therapists to give a clear lead in addressing life and death issues, especially in relation to wars, violence, the threat of climate emergency and the depletion of biodiversity.  How can we work with atavistic fears, when they present themselves to us in new guises? How can we face these challenges and refuse to give in to the banality of evil that Hannah Arendt spoke of?  Sinking into nihilism and wiping away the entire horizon, as Nietzsche put it so poetically in his Zarathustra is not the way to tame the dangers we are encountering.  We can only address our contemporary predicaments if we are willing to refuel our depleted capacity for feeling inspired and enthusiastic.  We need to set the bar higher and rediscover a wider perspective, together with our capacity for being in awe and wonder and for being creative, cooperative and communicative with each other, re-establishing values that direct us towards love and truth and freedom rather than competition, profit and hatred. It helps greatly to tackle these issues in a systematic way and to be aware of the structures of human existence, which always takes place on the same dimensions.

We are all torn between the search for pleasure and the fear of pain.

We all live on the physical dimension, where our body interacts with nature and the things in this world. We are all torn between the search for pleasure and the fear of pain. We also all live on a social dimension, where our personality interacts with a world of other people, who have created established rules and regulations and we can feel torn between our need to belong and a desire for isolation.  Each of us has an inner world, in which we seek to organize our selfhood and sense of identity, by taming our thoughts and feelings and where we are navigating between a desire for certainty and a craving for freedom. We also are faced with a spiritual dimension, which exposes us to the need to makes sense of the world in some way and find meaning by formulating values and finding inspiration and direction by discovering purpose or struggling with a sense of triviality and boredom. People are vulnerable when they have not got a clear idea about how life works and they often find it hard to see why they are stagnating or failing to find their way in the world.

The way forward

We know that people’s personal lives can also be blighted by external events or political changes and it is important to facilitate people’s understanding about such experiences. We can help them face up to these new, difficult realities with resilience, we can train them to be prepared for such eventualities and become more savvy in living. We know that the same things that divide people around the world, also unite us.  People across the globe are facing the same natural and human challenges, even though we each live on different continents and come from different cultural traditions.  We are different and disparate, yet each of us can feel disenfranchised and desperate in very similar ways.  We compete for the same resources and safety, but when we share these, we discover that there is enough for each of us.  We tread on each other's toes and easily come to fear each other, yet we are capable of loving, teaching, learning and understanding each other.

We need a philosophical framework to help mend the world and heal the wounds of the earth and the creatures on it.  This will become increasingly important as our established patterns, routines, and habits will be upset by further future catastrophic events, which will involve more loss, sorrow, confusion, fear, anger, doubt, anxiety and panic.

Existential therapists know how to bring people back from the brink of disaster, to find new courage.

To move forward from this place of perplexity and chaos towards a place of hope and confidence requires us to be robust in finding a clear and steady path and a strong sense of direction and purpose. We know that dystopic situations tend to lead towards alt-right power takeovers, because when people are afraid, they cling to leaders who use populist language and promise the moon and the stars, but who are pursuing their own agenda instead of thinking about what is best for humanity. How can we find the necessary inspiration and self-assurance not to fall into that post-truth trap? How do we teach people to reaffirm and value freedom and fairness and joy, even when all seems doom laden and difficult? And how can we not just repair, but improve the structures of our broken lives when so much is becoming undone and dire?

SUGGESTED VIEWING Power, politics, and mental health With Joanna Kavenna, Aaron Bastani, Simon Wessely, Praveetha Patalay

Existential therapists know how to bring people back from the brink of disaster, to find new courage. They help people to find a passage way from existential crisis to existential courage. They know the importance of fair and frank dialogue, true speaking communication, and the re-building of community.  Existential therapists know that there is only one way forward and that is through the difficulties ahead of us, with care and gentleness, but with great and calm determination. Their expertise can guide us through a time of change, towards transformation, and a renewed sense of human transcendence. They also know that it is vital to have a sense of direction and purpose in that process, if human beings are to rebuild a life that is meaningful and worthwhile and that will bring back a feeling of inspiration and enthusiasm which allows them to love life once again.
